instruction:
Class: Standard 4
Subject: Mathematics
Chapter Name: Chapter 1 – Shapes Around Us

1. Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, students should be able to:
1.	Identify different geometrical shapes.
2.	Understand the difference between 2D and 3D shapes.
3.	Recognise different types of prisms and pyramids.
4.	Understand faces, edges and vertices of solid shapes.
5.	Identify acute, right and obtuse angles.
6.	Understand the basic parts of a circle.
7.	Recognise geometrical patterns in everyday objects.
8.	Develop logical thinking and problem-solving skills.

2. Detailed Chapter-wise Teaching Plan
Lesson 1: Introduction to Shapes Around Us
Objective: To introduce students to geometrical shapes and their presence in buildings and monuments.
Online teaching procedure:
1.	I will begin by introducing the chapter.
2.	I will display the chapter's introductory videos.
3.	I will show pictures of famous monuments such as India Gate, Qutub Minar and other buildings.
4.	I will ask the student to observe the structures and identify the different shapes used in them.

Questions to ask the student:
•	What shapes can you identify in India Gate?
•	Why do buildings have different shapes?
•	Can you identify any geometrical shapes in the picture?
Expected learning outcome: The student will understand how geometrical shapes are used in buildings and everyday structures.
Activity 1: Shape Detective – Find the Hidden Shapes
Find a shape - Shape City by Eunoia | TPT
teacherspayteachers.com
How the activity works:
•	Display a colourful picture of a city, playground or building on the screen.
•	Ask students to observe the picture carefully.
•	Give them 30 seconds to find different geometrical shapes hidden in the picture.
•	Students must click on or identify the objects containing those shapes.
Questions:
•	Can you find a circular object?
•	Can you identify a rectangular window?
•	Which object looks like a triangle?
•	Can you find an object with a pyramid-like structure?
Learning outcome: Students develop observation skills and learn to recognise geometrical shapes in their surroundings.
Activity 2: Guess the Shape – Mystery Picture
How the activity works:
•	Show a zoomed-in or partially covered picture of an object.
•	Give the student three clues.
•	The student guesses the object and identifies its shape.
Example:
1.	I have four equal sides.
2.	I have four corners.
3.	A chessboard has many of my smaller forms.
Answer: Square.
Learning outcome: Improves logical thinking and shape recognition.

Lesson 2: Understanding 3D Shapes – Prisms and Pyramids
Objective: To help students recognise different 3D shapes and understand their properties.
Understanding 3D Shapes: Prisms and Pyramids

General Concept: Prisms
[Video Format: Animated Slide Presentation - Prisms Overview]
•	A prism has two identical and parallel bases facing each other.
•	The side faces connect the two bases together.
•	Examples include triangular, square, and hexagonal prisms.

1. Triangular Prism
[Video Format: 3D Illustration & Slide Presentation - Triangular Prism]
•	It features two identical, parallel triangular bases at opposite ends
•	It is enclosed by three rectangular side faces connecting the bases
•	It has a total of 5 faces, 9 edges, and 6 vertices.

2. Square Prism
[Video Format: 3D Illustration & Slide Presentation - Square Prism]
•	It features two identical, parallel square bases at the top and bottom.
•	It has four rectangular side faces connecting the two bases.
•	A cube is a special type of square prism where all dimensions (length, width, and height) are equal.

3. Hexagonal Prism
[Video Format: 3D Illustration & Slide Presentation - Hexagonal Prism]
•	It features two identical, parallel hexagonal bases with six sides each.
•	It is enclosed by six rectangular side faces connecting the top and bottom bases.
•	It contains a total of 8 faces, 18 edges, and 12 vertices.

General Concept: Pyramids
[Video Format: Animated Slide Presentation - Pyramids Overview]

•	A pyramid has one single flat base.
•	Its triangular side faces slant upward and meet at one common point called the apex.
•	Examples include triangular, square, and pentagonal pyramids.

4. Triangular Pyramid
[Video Format: 3D Illustration & Slide Presentation - Triangular Pyramid]

•	It has a single triangular base and three triangular side faces.
•	All faces of the shape (including the base) are triangles.
•	It has a total of 4 faces, 6 edges, and 4 vertices meeting at the top apex.

5. Square Pyramid
[Video Format: 3D Illustration & Slide Presentation - Square Pyramid]
•	It features a single flat square base at the bottom.
•	It has four triangular side faces that slant upward to a single apex point.
•	It contains a total of 5 faces, 8 edges, and 5 vertices.

I will explain the difference between these two concepts ( Image)
Prisms:
•	A prism has two identical and parallel bases.
•	The side faces connect the two bases.
•	Examples include triangular, square and hexagonal prisms.
Pyramids:
•	A pyramid has one base.
•	Its triangular side faces meet at one common point called the apex.
•	Examples include triangular, square and pentagonal pyramids.


Lesson 2: Understanding 3D Shapes – Prisms and Pyramids
Activity 1: Match the 3D Shape
Names Of Prisms Shapes at Scarlett Packham blog
How the activity works:
•	Display different 3D shapes on the left side of the screen.
•	Display their names on the right side in a mixed order.
•	Students must drag the correct name and drop it below the corresponding shape.
Examples:
3D shape	Name
Triangular prism	Triangular Prism
Square pyramid	Square Pyramid
Cube	Cube
Hexagonal prism	Hexagonal Prism
Triangular pyramid	Triangular Pyramid
Learning outcome: Students learn to identify and differentiate between different solid shapes.
Activity 2: Build Your Own 3D Shape – Virtual Blocks Challenge
☔장마집콕특가☔ ♥자석블럭세트♥ 베어블리 자석블럭 큐브 set - 베어블리 BEARVELY
How the activity works:
•	Provide students with a digital collection of blocks.
•	Allow them to drag, rotate and arrange the blocks on a virtual building area.
•	Give them a challenge to construct a prism or pyramid or different shapes using the available blocks.
•	Once completed, ask them to identify the shape they have constructed.
Challenges:
1.	Build a structure resembling a triangular prism.
2.	Arrange blocks to create a square-based pyramid.
3.	Build a cube using smaller unit cubes.
Learning outcome: Students develop spatial understanding and learn how 3D shapes are constructed.
Activity 3: Prism or Pyramid? – Quick Sorting Game
How the activity works:
•	Display different 3D shapes one by one.
•	Give students two virtual baskets labelled Prism and Pyramid.
•	Students drag each shape into the correct basket.
•	Show immediate feedback after each answer.
Learning outcome: Students understand the difference between prisms and pyramids through classification.

Lesson 3: Understanding Nets of 3D Shapes
Objective: To explain how a flat two-dimensional pattern can be folded to form a three-dimensional shape.
Create a video-style script explaining Lesson 3 ("Understanding Nets of 3D Shapes") like a story. Describe how you would explain what a net is, how flat patterns fold into 3D shapes, and showcase the digital illustrations of nets for cubes, cuboids, prisms, and pyramids.
I will first display the net of a cube and explain how its connected squares fold to form a cube. (Slide)
Nets Of 3D Shapes Lesson at Anthony Soto blog
I will explain:
•	A net is a flat pattern that can be folded to form a 3D shape.
•	Different 3D shapes have different nets.
•	The faces of the net form the surfaces of the final solid shape.
I will display nets of cubes, cuboids, prisms and pyramids through digital illustrations.
Lesson 3: Understanding Nets of 3D Shapes
Activity 1: Fold It! – 2D to 3D Challenge
Planificações do cubo, no GeoGebra | Estudo Autónomo
How the activity works:
•	Display an unfolded net of a cube on the screen.
•	Provide virtual folding lines.
•	Students click on the sides to fold them upwards.
•	The flat net gradually transforms into a 3D cube.
•	Repeat with a cuboid or pyramid net.
Learning outcome: Students understand how a 2D net transforms into a 3D solid shape.

Activity 2: Which Net Makes Which Shape?
How the activity works:
•	Display different nets on the left side.
•	Display 3D shapes on the right side.
•	Ask students to match each net with its corresponding solid shape.
For example:
•	Six connected squares → Cube.
•	Six rectangles → Cuboid (using a suitable cuboid net).
•	One square and four triangles → Square pyramid.
Learning outcome: Students develop the ability to recognise and visualise nets of solid shapes.

Activity 3: Find the Wrong Net!
How the activity works:
•	Display three different nets.
•	Two nets will fold into the given solid shape.
•	One net will not form that shape.
•	Students must select the incorrect net and explain why.
Learning outcome: Improves spatial reasoning and problem-solving skills.

Lesson 4: Faces, Edges and Corners
Objective: To identify the faces, edges and corners of solid shapes.
Create a video-style script explaining Lesson 4 ("Faces, Edges and Corners") using a digital whiteboard demonstration of a cube. Define faces, edges, and corners (vertices) clearly, and walk through the exact counts for a cube (6 faces, 12 edges, and 8 corners) so students can easily identify and count them.
Properties of 3D Shapes - KS3 Maths - BBC Bitesize
I will explain:
•	Face: A flat surface of a 3D shape.
•	Edge: The line where two faces meet.
•	Corner (Vertex): The point where edges meet.
I will use a cube as an example and explain:
Property	Number
Faces	6
Edges	12
Corners	8
Expected learning outcome: The student will be able to identify and count faces, edges and corners.

Lesson 4: Understanding Faces, Edges and Corners
Activity 1: Label the Cube – Find Its Parts
What are 3D shapes? - BBC Bitesize
How the activity works:
•	Display a large 3D cube on the screen.
•	Provide three labels: Face, Edge and Vertex.
•	Students drag each label to the correct part of the cube.
•	When they click on a face, edge or vertex, that part gets highlighted.
Learning outcome: Students understand the difference between faces, edges and vertices.

Activity 2: Count and Win – 3D Shape Challenge
How the activity works:
•	Display different 3D shapes, such as cubes, cuboids, triangular prisms and square pyramids.
•	Ask students to count their faces, edges and vertices.
•	Give three answer boxes for each shape.
•	Students enter their answers and receive instant feedback.
Example challenge:
Shape	Faces	Edges	Vertices
Cube	6	12	8
Cuboid	6	12	8
Triangular prism	5	9	6
Square pyramid	5	8	5
Learning outcome: Students practise counting and identifying the properties of 3D shapes.

Activity 3: Spin the Shape – Explore in 3D
How the activity works usind a dice:
•	Display a rotatable 3D cube or cuboid.
•	Allow students to rotate the object using their mouse controls.
•	Ask them to identify the faces visible from different directions.
•	Ask questions such as: How many faces can you see now? What happens when you rotate the cube?
Learning outcome: Students understand that a 3D object has different visible faces depending on its position.

Lesson 5: Understanding Cube Towers and Geometrical Drawings
Objective: To develop spatial understanding and help students visualise how cubes are arranged to form different structures.
Create a video-style script for Lesson 5 ("Understanding Cube Towers and Geometrical Drawings") focusing on spatial visualization. Demonstrate how individual cubes combine in rows and columns, explain how to count cubes in stacked structures, and use a animation with an isometric grid to show step-by-step how to sketch 3D cube arrangements.
Isometric Cube Drawing at PaintingValley.com | Explore collection of Isometric Cube Drawing
I will explain:
•	How cubes are arranged in rows and columns.
•	How the position of each cube affects the overall structure.
•	How to count the cubes in a given arrangement.
•	How to represent a 3D structure through a drawing.

Lesson 5: Understanding Cube Towers and Geometrical Drawings
Activity 1: Build a Cube Tower – Virtual Construction Challenge
Betzold Würfel aus Holz, 100 Stück | betzold.de
How the activity works:
•	Provide a virtual collection of small cubes.
•	Students drag and drop cubes to construct different towers.
•	Give them specific challenges:
1.	Build a tower with three cubes.
2.	Build a structure with two cubes at the bottom and one on top.
3.	Build a structure with six cubes.
•	Ask students to count the total number of cubes used.
Learning outcome: Students understand how smaller cubes combine to form larger structures.

Activity 2: Look Carefully – How Many Cubes?
How the activity works:
•	Display a 3D arrangement of cubes on the screen.
•	Ask students to count all the cubes, including the partially hidden ones.
•	Give four multiple-choice answers.
•	Students select the correct answer.
Learning outcome: Develops spatial visualisation and logical reasoning.

Activity 3: Copy the Cube Structure
How the activity works:
•	Display a sample cube arrangement.
•	Give the student an empty virtual grid with draggable cubes.
•	Students must recreate the same structure.
•	Compare the student's construction with the original model.
Learning outcome: Improves visual observation, spatial understanding and accuracy.

Lesson 6: Understanding Angles
Objective: To identify different types of angles and understand how angles are formed.
Create a video-style script for Lesson 6 ("Understanding Angles") introducing how angles are formed by two rays meeting at a common endpoint. Demonstrate acute, right, and obtuse angles using interactive digital drawing tools and explain these concepts.

I will then demonstrate three types of angles using digital diagrams.
1. Acute Angle
Lines And Angles - Definition, Types, Properties
An angle smaller than a right angle.
Example: 45°.

2. Right Angle
Angle - Geometry
An angle equal to 90°.
Example: The corner of a square.

3. Obtuse Angle
DK Learning: Make every lesson your best yet
An angle greater than 90° but smaller than 180°.
Example: 120°.

Lesson 6: Understanding Angles
Activity 1: Angle Builder – Move and Make an Angle
Interactive Angles | Teaching Resources
How the activity works:
•	Display two movable arms joined at one endpoint.
•	Students can drag one arm to change the angle.
•	Show the angle measurement as the arm moves.
•	Ask students to create:
o	An acute angle.
o	A right angle.
o	An obtuse angle.
Learning outcome: Students understand how angles change and learn to identify different types of angles.


Activity 2: Angle Sorting Game
How the activity works:
•	Display different angles on the screen.
•	Provide three virtual boxes labelled:
o	Acute angle
o	Right angle
o	Obtuse angle
•	Students drag each angle into the correct box.
Include angles such as 30°, 45°, 90°, 110°, 120° and 150°.
Learning outcome: Students become confident in classifying angles.

Activity 3: Beat the Clock – Identify the Angle!
How the activity works:
•	Display one angle at a time.
•	Give the student five seconds to identify its type.
•	Provide three answer options.
•	Award one point for every correct answer.
•	Display the final score at the end.
Learning outcome: Improves quick identification and understanding of angles.

Lesson 7: Understanding Circles and Pentagons
Objective: To introduce the basic properties of circles and regular pentagons.
Create a video-style script for Lesson 7 ("Understanding Circles and Pentagons") using animation. Explain the key parts of a circle (centre, radius, and diameter), and introduce regular pentagons by covering their five sides, five corners, equal side lengths, and equal interior angles.
I will use the presentation slides to demonstrate the different parts of a circle.
Circles - Formulas, Properties | What is a Circle? | Examples
I will explain:
•	Centre: The point in the middle of a circle.
•	Radius: A line segment from the centre to the circle's boundary.
•	Diameter: A line segment passing through the centre and joining two points on the circle.
I will explain that a pentagon is a polygon with five sides and five corners. I will also demonstrate how a regular pentagon has five equal sides and five equal angles.

Lesson 7: Understanding Circles and Pentagons
Activity 1: Circle Detective – Label the Parts
Circles - Formulas, Properties | What is a Circle? | Examples
cuemath.com
How the activity works:
•	Display a large circle with its centre, radius and diameter marked but not labelled.
•	Provide three labels: Centre, Radius and Diameter.
•	Students drag the labels to their correct positions.
•	After completing the activity, show the correct answers.
Learning outcome: Students understand and identify the important parts of a circle.
Activity 2: Radius or Diameter? – Quick Challenge
How the activity works:
•	Display different circles with measurements.
•	Ask students to calculate the missing radius or diameter.
•	Students enter the answer in a digital answer box.
Example:
1.	Radius = 3 cm. Find the diameter.
2.	Diameter = 10 cm. Find the radius.
3.	Radius = 7 cm. Find the diameter.
Learning outcome: Students practise the relationship between radius and diameter.
Activity 3: Build a Pentagon
Area of a Pentagon | Definition, Facts, Example & Quiz
workybooks.com
How the activity works:
•	Provide five draggable line segments and five movable points.
•	Ask students to connect them to form a pentagon.
•	Allow students to select the corners and count the sides.
•	Show a regular pentagon and an irregular pentagon for comparison.
Learning outcome: Students understand that a pentagon has five sides and five vertices and recognise regular and irregular pentagons.

Lesson 8: Shapes with Straws – Understanding Rigidity
Objective: To understand why triangles are considered rigid shapes.
Create an animated video-style script for Lesson 8 ("Shapes with Straws – Understanding Rigidity") using digital illustrations of shapes made from connected straws. Demonstrate why a triangle is a rigid shape that resists changing its form when pushed, and contrast it with a rectangular straw frame that easily flexes and deforms into a slanted quadrilateral with changing angles.
I will use animated diagrams or digital illustrations of triangles and rectangles made using connected straws.
Corrugation Nation | Exploratorium
Parallelogram activity frame teaching – Boardgames and Puzzles
Exploring Structural Engineering Fundamentals Strength of Shapes Shapes

I will explain:
•	A triangle is a rigid shape.
•	When a triangle is pushed, its shape does not easily change if its side lengths remain fixed.
•	A rectangle can change into a slanted quadrilateral when pushed.
•	The angles of the rectangle change when its shape changes.
I will demonstrate this transformation through a digital animation or sequential drawings on the whiteboard.
Expected learning outcome: The student will understand the concept of rigidity through visual demonstration and reasoning.

Lesson 8: Shapes with Straws – Understanding Rigidity
Activity 1: Triangle vs Rectangle – Which One Is Stronger?
Notes for A3.2.8 Strengthening techniques in structures - IB | RevisionDojo
revisiondojo.com
How the activity works:
•	Display a virtual triangle and rectangle made using connected line segments.
•	Allow students to drag one corner of each shape.
•	When they drag the rectangle, its shape changes into a slanted quadrilateral.
•	When they try the same with the triangle while keeping its side lengths fixed, its shape remains unchanged.
•	Ask students which shape is more rigid.
Learning outcome: Students understand why triangles provide rigidity in structures.

Activity 2: Build a Strong Structure – Shape Construction Game
How the activity works:
•	Provide virtual sticks and joining points.
•	Ask students to build a square-shaped frame.
•	Next, ask them to add a diagonal stick to the square.
•	Let them compare the stability of the structure before and after adding the diagonal.
•	Ask why the additional diagonal makes the structure more rigid.
Learning outcome: Students understand how triangles help strengthen structures.

Activity 3: True or False – Rigidity Quiz
How the activity works:
Display statements one by one and let students select True or False.
1.	A triangle is a rigid shape. (True)
2.	A rectangle can change its shape when pushed. (True)
3.	A triangle has four sides. (False)
4.	Adding a diagonal to a rectangular frame creates two triangles. (True)
Learning outcome: Reinforces the concept of rigidity through a quick interactive quiz.

Lesson 9: Revision and Chapter Practice
Create a video-style script for Lesson 9 ("Revision and Chapter Practice") summarizing a comprehensive online review session. Walk through revisiting key concepts with presentation slides, running a shape-identification visual quiz, assigning a digital worksheet and online assessment to evaluate student mastery.
•	Revisit the important concepts using the presentation slides.
•	Show diagrams and ask the student to identify shapes.
•	Provide a digital worksheet.
•	Conduct a short online assessment.
This will help me evaluate the student's understanding before moving to the next chapter.
